title: Shloka 146
subtitle: Perishable and imperishable, and a line built out of threes

namas.gloss: Whose Being Is Perishable And Imperishable
namas.translation: What decays and what never decays are both her, so that nothing falls outside her nature.

morphology.note: In ātmikā the -ka suffix already means having, so the word is taken as a derivative of kṣarākṣarātman; a bahuvrīhi reading, she whose self is the perishable and the imperishable, is also current.

compound.gloss: consisting of the perishable and the imperishable

children.gloss: having the nature of, consisting of

namas.translation: Every world, high or low, has her for its one sovereign.
She carries the whole world, and it stays in being only because she keeps holding it.

compound.gloss: she who bears up the universe

namas.translation: Right conduct, means and pleasure — the three ends a person may honourably pursue — are all in her gift.

compound.gloss: bestower of the group of three human aims

namas.translation: Good fortune is her permanent condition, and it shows as beauty and as the power to make others fortunate.
Sun, moon and fire are her three eyes, so that she sees by day, by night and past both.

namas.gloss: Whose Nature Is The Three Strands
namas.translation: Purity, energy and inertia are the three threads she is spun from, and she weaves the world out of them.

morphology.note: The possessive force belongs to the -ka of ātmaka, so triguṇātman is the compound proper; read the other way the name is a bahuvrīhi, she whose nature is the three strands.

children.gloss: a strand of a cord; a constituent quality of nature
having the nature of, consisting of

commentary.meaning: After a verse of myth the hymn goes back to argument. The first line makes three statements of scope, each larger in its way than the last: she consists of both the perishable and the imperishable, she rules every world there is, she holds the universe up. The order matters, because it moves from what she is made of, to what she governs, to what she does — and the third is a present-tense activity, not a completed act, since dhāriṇī means the one who is holding, now. The second line then turns over into threes. Three of its four names begin with tri-: the giver of the three human aims, the three-eyed, the one whose nature is the three strands out of which the world is spun. Between them sits subhagā, the only name in the verse that could be said of an ordinary woman, and the only one that promises anything as small as good luck. The root bhaga has now surfaced three times in four verses — as the misfortune she scatters, as the sea of fortune she lights, and here as her own settled condition — which is one of the quieter pieces of design in this part of the stotra.
commentary.history:
Kṣara and akṣara are technical terms with a specific home, and any reader who knows the Bhagavad Gītā will hear the fifteenth chapter behind the first name. There the Gītā declares that there are two puruṣas in the world, the perishable and the imperishable: the perishable is all beings, and the imperishable is what stands unmoved at the summit. It then adds a third above both, the supreme puruṣa who is called the highest self. The sahasranāma does something different with the same pair. It does not put her above the two; the suffix -ātmikā says that she consists of them, has them for her substance. The name is read both ways, as a tatpuruṣa (she who is made of the perishable and the imperishable) and as a possessive compound (she whose self they are), and the difference is small in effect but real in emphasis. The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, which is the other great source for this vocabulary, keeps the terms apart and has the one god rule over both; the hymn refuses even that separation. Akṣara is also the ordinary word for a syllable, so that the word for what does not decay is the same one by which this school's fifteen-syllabled mantra is counted.

Loka, in the second name, is the general word for a world or sphere of existence, and the standard cosmology counts fourteen of them, seven above and seven below, from the earth up to the world of truth and down to Pātāla. Sarvalokeśī claims all of them without distinguishing. The feminine īśī is a plainer formation than the maheśvarī of the previous verse or the more usual īśānī, and reads as a flat statement rather than a title.

Viśvadhāriṇī rests on the root dhṛ, to hold or support, from which dharma also comes: dharma is, etymologically, what holds things together. The name therefore prepares the one that follows it, where dharma heads the list of gifts. What is asserted is not that she made the universe at some past moment but that she is bearing it now, and that if the holding stopped there would be nothing left standing. Purāṇic imagination gives this work to the serpent Śeṣa and to the elephants of the quarters; the name assigns it to her without machinery.

Trivarga is a term of the legal and political literature: the group of three, meaning dharma, artha and kāma — right conduct, the means of life, and pleasure. These are three of the four puruṣārthas, the ends a human being may properly pursue, and the classical texts argue at length about their ranking, Manu among them. The fourth end, liberation, is regularly set apart under the name apavarga. It is characteristic of this hymn that it says trivarga and means it, promising the goods of a lived life in the middle of a long passage about the removal of suffering.

Subhagā means simply one who has a fair portion. Bhaga is a share or allotment and also the Āditya who allots it, and the word runs deep in Sanskrit: bhagavat, the standard title for a god, means one who possesses bhaga, which the Purāṇic definition unpacks as sovereignty, righteousness, fame, beauty, knowledge and dispassion. The derived form saubhāgya is everywhere in this tradition — it names the school's own vidyā, and it names Bhāskararāya's commentary on this very hymn.

Tryambakā is the feminine of one of Śiva's oldest names, the one invoked in the Vedic verse that has become the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra. The usual explanation takes ambaka as eye and gives three-eyed: the sun, the moon and fire, so that she sees by day, by night, and past both. Commentators also note that ambā means mother and offer three mothers as an alternative reading of the old name. Taking a name of Śiva into the feminine is a habit of this hymn — Maheśvarī two lines earlier does the same — and it is not grammatical politeness but the school's central claim.

The last name is Sāṃkhya. Guṇa means a strand of a rope before it means anything else, and the three strands are sattva, rajas and tamas: clarity, motion and inertia. In classical Sāṃkhya, prakṛti is nothing but these three, held in equilibrium until the equilibrium is disturbed and the world unfolds. Śākta theology takes prakṛti to be her, which makes triguṇātmikā an identification rather than a metaphor. The Devī Māhātmya's framing assigns one guṇa to each of its three presiding forms, with the dark form this hymn called Mahākālī one verse earlier standing for tamas. Read against the name of the school's deity, Tripurasundarī, the beautiful one of the three cities, the second half of the verse looks less like a list than a tour of a single number.
commentary.practice:
The two lines divide differently and this catches people out. In the first line the names run six, five and five syllables, so the caesura after the eighth syllable lands two syllables inside sarvalokeśī; do not breathe there, and carry the line whole. In the second line the first two names come to exactly eight, so the break falls cleanly after subhagā. One line resists the pause, the other invites it.

Kṣarākṣarātmikā looks forbidding and is mostly sandhi. The parts are kṣara, akṣara and ātmikā; a final a meeting an initial a gives a single long ā, and a final a meeting a long ā gives the same, so two joins disappear into two long vowels and the word contracts to what you see. The cluster kṣ occurs twice and is a single conjunct, k released directly into the retroflex ṣ. Regional practice varies in how far back that sibilant is made, but it should not become the palatal ś. The ending -ātmikā has t and m together, a combination English never puts inside a syllable; give the t a real closure before the m.

Viśvadhāriṇī offers a rule worth learning once and applying everywhere. The ṇ is retroflex because of the r earlier in the word, even though a long ī stands between them. The same rule produced aparṇā in the previous verse at close range, and it produces kāriṇī, dhāraṇā and a hundred other forms at a distance. Once you expect it, you will stop being surprised by retroflex nasals in words that seem to have nothing to trigger them.

Tryambakā is the hardest syllable in the verse. Trya is one syllable, not two: t, r and y released together and then the vowel, followed by mba with the labial nasal closing onto the aspirate-free b. Reciters who have learned the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra will already have the shape in their mouths from tryambakaṃ yajāmahe, and it is worth saying that line once before attempting the name.

In archanā the verse mixes the two feminine datives again, and the ī-stems are the ones to watch: sarvalokeśyai namaḥ, viśvadhāriṇyai namaḥ, trivargadātryai namaḥ, where the long ī shortens to a glide before the ending. Dātrī is an agent noun in -tṛ turned feminine, the same formation as in dātā and kartā, and its dative dātryai is worth fixing separately because the pattern recurs. The others are regular: kṣarākṣarātmikāyai, subhagāyai, tryambakāyai, triguṇātmikāyai.

What the verse asks is chiefly a matter of not flinching at the first name. It is easy to say that the imperishable is her. The name says that the perishable is her too — that what is dissolving, including the reciter, is not outside her nature and does not need to be redeemed into something else before it can be. The second line then asks something almost opposite: to admit wanting the ordinary goods, since the reciter who says trivargadātrī is asking for conduct, means and pleasure by name, and subhagā simply describes good fortune as her condition. There is no embarrassment in the verse about any of this, and there is no reason for the reciter to supply any.

crossReferences.translation: There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable is all beings; the one who stands unmoved at the peak is called the imperishable.
crossReferences.relevance: The passage that fixed this vocabulary, and the measure of what the hymn's first name is doing. The Gītā separates the two and then places a third above them, the supreme person who is neither. Kṣarākṣarātmikā declines the ascent: instead of a third term standing over the pair, she is said to consist of the pair. Anyone who wants to see the difference between a theology of transcendence and a theology of identity can compare these two formulations and need not look further.

crossReferences.translation: We make offering to the three-eyed one, the fragrant, who increases nourishment. As a cucumber is freed from its stem, may I be freed from death — not from deathlessness.
crossReferences.relevance: The source of the name, and one of the most widely recited verses in Sanskrit, used for the sick and the dying. Tryambakā in the sahasranāma is its feminine, and the transfer is not decorative: the verses immediately preceding this one in the hymn have been about disease and death, and the Vedic verse behind this name is the one Hindus actually say at a sickbed. The final phrase is exact and often mistranslated — release from death, but not from what does not die.

crossReferences.translation: One unborn female, red and white and black, giving birth to many offspring shaped like herself; one unborn male lies with her in enjoyment, and another unborn male leaves her when her pleasures have been used up.
crossReferences.relevance: The verse the Sāṃkhya tradition took as scriptural warrant for the doctrine behind triguṇātmikā, reading the three colours as the three strands and the unborn female as prakṛti herself. The riddle also exposes what Śākta theology had to change: in the Upaniṣad the female principle is what the male leaves behind, whereas the sahasranāma makes her the subject of the whole hymn and the three strands simply what she is composed of.

references.title: Classical Sāṃkhya: An Interpretation of Its History and Meaning
references.author: Gerald James Larson (Motilal Banarsidass, 2nd ed.)
references.note: The clearest account of what the guṇas are supposed to be — not qualities that something has, but the constituents that something is — which is the distinction triguṇātmikā turns on. Larson also prints and translates the Sāṃkhyakārikā, seventy-odd verses that take an evening and will make dozens of names in this hymn legible.

references.title: Upaniṣads
references.author: tr. Patrick Olivelle (Oxford World's Classics, 1996)
references.note: The translation to use if you are going to check a quotation. Olivelle is exact about what is and is not in the text, notes where the readings are uncertain, and does not smooth the older prose into edifying English. The Śvetāśvatara, source of both the kṣara/akṣara vocabulary and the riddle of the three-coloured unborn female, is short enough to read at one sitting.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: Read this for the triads. Brooks lays out why threeness organizes so much of Śrīvidyā — the three segments of the mantra, the three cities of Tripurā, the three goddesses, the three eyes — and it is the background against which the second line of this verse stops looking like an accident of vocabulary.

references.title: Manu's Code of Law: A Critical Edition and Translation of the Mānava-Dharmaśāstra
references.author: Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 2005)
references.note: For trivarga. The second book contains the classic discussion of how dharma, artha and kāma are to be ranked against one another, with the competing opinions set out and adjudicated. It is the best short way to see that the three aims were a live argument rather than a pious formula, and therefore that trivargadātrī is granting something contested.
